name: Swayambhunath
tagline: Hilltop stupa above Kathmandu, reached by 365 stone steps
meta_description: Swayambhunath guide: the 365-step east stairway, the monkeys, Harati temple, sunset over Kathmandu, Amideva Buddha Park, entry fee and how to get there.
summary: Swayambhunath is a hilltop stupa 3 km west of Thamel, one of the oldest Buddhist sites in Nepal and a UNESCO monument zone. You climb 365 stone steps past monkeys and shrines to a gilded tower painted with the Buddha's eyes, then look out over the whole Kathmandu Valley.
intro: The Kathmandu Valley's own creation story begins on this hill. According to the Swayambhu Purana the valley was once a lake, a lotus bloomed on its waters and gave off a self-created light, and the bodhisattva Manjushri cut a gorge at Chobhar to drain the water so that people could reach it. Where the lotus settled, the hill of Swayambhu rose. A medieval chronicle credits the first stupa to King Vrishadeva around the start of the fifth century, which makes this one of the oldest religious sites in the valley.

Today the white dome is crowned by a gilded square tower painted on all four sides with the Buddha's half-closed eyes, a third eye above them and a curled symbol below that looks like a question mark: it is the Nepali numeral one, standing for unity. Around the stupa crowd shrines, prayer wheels, butter lamp houses, a Tibetan monastery and the pagoda of Harati, protector of children, worshipped by Buddhists and Hindus alike. That mix of the two faiths on one hilltop is typical of the valley's Newar culture.

Most visitors know it as the Monkey Temple. Troops of rhesus macaques live on the wooded slopes, which legend says grew from lice in Manjushri's hair, and they slide down the stair rails and raid unattended bags. The climb is part of the experience: 365 steps on the east side, rising roughly 70 m, with a gentler western entrance for those who cannot manage it. Foreign visitors pay an entry fee of around NPR 200, with a lower SAARC rate; check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: The 365-step east stairway
highlights.text: The traditional approach starts at a gate with three large painted Buddha statues and climbs 365 worn stone steps through the trees, past carved animals and small chaityas. It takes 15 to 25 minutes with stops. At the top you step out beside a massive gilded vajra, the thunderbolt symbol of Vajrayana Buddhism, facing the stupa.

highlights.title: The stupa and its eyes
highlights.text: Up close the stupa is ringed by prayer wheels and gilded niches holding images of the five Buddhas. The eyes on the tower watch the valley in all four directions, and the thirteen gilded rings above them stand for the stages toward enlightenment. Walk around it clockwise, spinning each wheel with your right hand.

highlights.title: Harati temple and the shrines
highlights.text: Beside the stupa stands the small pagoda of Harati, goddess of children and protector against disease, where mothers bring babies for blessings. Around the platform are the two tall stone shikhara temples built in the 17th century under King Pratap Malla, rows of chaityas and a Tibetan gompa where monks chant in the afternoons.

highlights.title: A view over the whole valley
highlights.text: From the eastern terraces the city spreads out below: the rebuilt Dharahara tower, the old core around Durbar Square, the airport and the hills of the valley rim. On clear mornings from October to February, Ganesh Himal and the Langtang peaks show to the north above the haze.

highlights.title: The Monkey Temple crowd
highlights.text: Hundreds of rhesus macaques live on the hill and have no fear of people. Watching the young ones play on the railings and fountains is a favourite with children, but do not feed them, keep food and drinks in a closed bag, and give mothers with babies plenty of space.

highlights.title: Amideva Buddha Park at the foot
highlights.text: On the western side of the hill, across the ring road, three golden statues of about 20 m tower over a small park: Amitabha, known locally as Amideva, in the centre, flanked by Shakyamuni Buddha and Avalokiteshvara. Locals walk a circuit around the hill here every morning, lined with prayer wheels and chortens.

how_to_reach.text: Swayambhunath is about 3 km west of Thamel, roughly 15 minutes by car. A taxi costs about NPR 300 to 400. Ask for the east gate if you want to climb the 365 steps, or the western car park if you want the shorter walk up; our cars use either, depending on who is in the group and what else is on the day's plan.

From Thamel it is a 40 to 50 minute walk through Chhetrapati and across the Bishnumati River, then along the lane to the east stairway. From Kathmandu Durbar Square it is about 2.5 km. Walking there in the early morning, when the city is just waking, makes a good start to the dawn climb.

Tribhuvan International Airport is about 8 km east, 30 to 45 minutes by road across the city depending on traffic. Swayambhunath works well on the morning after you arrive, combined with Kathmandu Durbar Square, which lies between the stupa and Thamel and is easily added on the way back.

where_to_stay: There are no large hotels on the hill itself, and few reasons to sleep beside it, because Thamel is only 3 km away. Most of our guests stay in a 3-star hotel in Thamel, which puts restaurants, shops and the walking route to the stupa on the doorstep. For more comfort, Hotel Shanker in Lazimpat and Hotel Yak & Yeti on Durbar Marg are 15 to 25 minutes by car, and the Kathmandu Marriott Hotel in Naxal is a little further east. A handful of small guesthouses around the Swayambhu and Chhauni area suit travellers who want to climb at first light without a taxi.
tips: Climb the east stairway early, before 8 am, when it is cooler, quieter and the monkeys are still sleepy.
Keep sunglasses, water bottles and snacks out of sight, as the monkeys snatch anything that looks like food.
Take the western entrance by car if anyone in your group has knee or heart trouble, as it saves most of the climb.
Wear shoes with grip, because the old stone steps are steep, uneven and slippery after rain.
Walk clockwise around the stupa and shrines, and keep a few NPR 10 and 20 notes for donations at the butter lamp houses.

experiences.title: Dawn climb up the Swayambhunath east stairway
experiences.best_time: 6–8:30 am, all year; Oct–Feb for clear views
experiences.summary: An early start from Thamel to climb the 365 steps of Swayambhunath's east stairway with the morning worshippers, reaching the stupa as the first butter lamps are lit and the valley below is still under mist. Breakfast follows at a cafe near the top.
body: We pick you up in Thamel at about 6 am, or walk the 3 km with you if you prefer, and start up the east stairway as the city wakes. At the base, three large painted statues of the Buddha mark the gate, and a few steps on a line of stone animals, the mounts of the five Buddhas, guards the path. Newar Buddhists and Tibetans climb at this hour with offerings of rice, flowers and incense, and many will greet you on the way.

The 365 steps rise roughly 70 m. We take it slowly, pausing at the small shrines and chaityas set into the slope, and you will meet the hill's monkeys coming down from the trees to warm themselves on the stones. At the top a huge gilded vajra sits on a drum carved with the animals of the Tibetan calendar. Beyond it, the stupa's eyes catch the first sun, and the smell of juniper smoke drifts across the platform.

We walk clockwise around the stupa, light butter lamps if you wish, and step into the Harati temple, where mothers bring babies for the goddess's blessing. By 7:30 am the mist is usually lifting off the valley, and from the eastern terraces you can pick out Durbar Square, the Dharahara tower and, in winter, the snow peaks to the north. We finish with breakfast at a cafe on the hill and are back in Thamel by about 8:30 am.

faqs.q: How many steps are there at Swayambhunath?
faqs.a: The east stairway has 365 stone steps, rising roughly 70 m from the gate to the stupa platform. Most people take 15 to 25 minutes with a few rests. The steps are steep and uneven in places, with handrails at the top section. A western entrance with a car park offers a much shorter climb.

faqs.q: What time does Swayambhunath open in the morning?
faqs.a: The hill is open to worshippers from very early, before sunrise, and many locals climb from around 5 am. Ticket booths for foreign visitors generally open by early morning, and you can enter for the dawn climb with a guide. Hours can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the dawn climb suitable for children?
faqs.a: Yes for children of about six and over who can manage a long flight of stairs with rests. Hold younger children's hands near the top, where the steps steepen, and keep snacks hidden from the monkeys. Families with toddlers or grandparents can take the car to the western entrance and still be on the platform for sunrise.

experiences.title: Sunset over Kathmandu from Swayambhunath
experiences.price_hint: ≈ ₹1,500 per person with car and guide
experiences.summary: A late-afternoon visit to Swayambhunath, timed so you reach the eastern terraces as the light turns gold on the city and the valley rim, then stay to watch Kathmandu's lights come on below. It is the easiest high viewpoint in the city.
body: We drive to the western car park around 4 pm in winter or 5 pm in spring and autumn, which saves the climb for those who want to arrive fresh, and walk the last few minutes up to the stupa. Your guide uses the first half hour to show you the platform: the stupa's niches, the Harati temple, the stone shikharas from the reign of Pratap Malla and the small gompa where monks often chant in the late afternoon.

Then we settle on the eastern terraces. Because the hill is on the western edge of the city, the sun drops behind you and lights up the whole valley in front, from the rooftops of Thamel and the old town to the white tower of Dharahara and the Shivapuri hills along the northern rim. From October to February the air is often clear enough to see Ganesh Himal and the Langtang peaks turn pink for a few minutes before the light goes.

As the city lights come on, the butter lamps around the stupa are lit and the evening kora slowly begins, mostly local families walking clockwise after work. We walk down the east stairway in the dusk, or return to the car if you prefer, and can drop you in Thamel or at a restaurant near Durbar Square for dinner. Bring a light jacket from November to February, as the hilltop cools quickly once the sun sets.

faqs.a: Yes, it is one of the best sunset spots in Kathmandu. The hill sits on the western edge of the city, so the setting sun lights the valley in front of you, and on clear winter evenings the Himalaya to the north glows pink. Arrive 45 minutes before sunset to get a good place on the eastern terraces.

faqs.q: Can you see the Himalaya from Swayambhunath?
faqs.a: On clear days, mostly from October to February, you can see Ganesh Himal and peaks of the Langtang range above the northern rim of the valley. In spring the haze usually hides them, and from June to September cloud does. The view over the city itself is good in every season except heavy rain.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk down the steps after dark?
faqs.a: Yes, with care. The east stairway is used by locals into the evening, but the lighting is patchy and the old steps are uneven, so a phone torch helps. Our guides walk down with you, or we return to the car at the western entrance. The monkeys are calmer after dark but still curious about bags.

experiences.title: Amideva Buddha Park and the hill circuit
experiences.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, all year
experiences.summary: A walk at the western foot of Swayambhunath through Amideva Buddha Park, with its three golden statues, then along the circuit around the hill that local devotees follow each morning, past prayer wheels, chortens and small shrines. It is flat, easy and quieter than the hilltop.
body: Most visitors see only the top of Swayambhu, but the life of the hill also runs around its base. We start at Amideva Buddha Park on the western side, just off the ring road, where three golden statues of about 20 m stand side by side: Amitabha, the Buddha of Infinite Light, known here as Amideva, in the centre, with Shakyamuni Buddha on one side and Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, on the other. Painted reliefs and smaller images line the walls around them.

From the park we join the circuit around the hill, the path that Newar and Tibetan Buddhists walk clockwise at dawn and dusk, often with prayer beads in hand. It passes long rows of prayer wheels, whitewashed chortens, stone carvings and small courtyards, and gives glimpses up the wooded slope to the stupa above. Your guide explains the five Buddhas of the Vajrayana tradition, their colours and gestures, and why you see them repeated all over the hill.

The walk covers a little over 2 km on mostly flat paths and paving, and suits seniors and young children. It takes about 1.5 hours with stops, and the park is free to enter, though donations at the shrines are welcome. Many guests add it before or after a visit to the stupa itself, using the western entrance to climb the short stair to the top, so the whole morning stays on foot.

faqs.a: Amideva Buddha Park lies at the western foot of the Swayambhunath hill, beside the ring road, about 10 minutes' walk from the western entrance to the stupa. It is roughly 3.5 km from Thamel, around 15 to 20 minutes by car. Many visitors combine it with the stupa on the same morning.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Amideva Buddha Park?
faqs.a: No ticket has been charged for the park itself, and it is open to everyone, though donations at the shrines are welcome. The main Swayambhunath entry fee applies only when you go up to the stupa platform. Rules can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Who are the three Buddhas at Amideva Buddha Park?
faqs.a: The central statue is Amitabha, the Buddha of Infinite Light, called Amideva in Nepal. On either side stand Shakyamuni, the historical Buddha born at Lumbini in Nepal, and Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion who is especially loved by Tibetan Buddhists. Your guide explains the gestures and symbols of each statue.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Swayambhunath?
faqs.a: Foreign visitors pay about NPR 200 to enter the stupa area, while SAARC nationals pay a lower rate and Nepalis enter free. Tickets are sold at both the east stairway and the western entrance. Fees change from time to time, so check current status before you travel. Keep your ticket until you leave the hill.

faqs.q: Why is Swayambhunath called the Monkey Temple?
faqs.a: Swayambhunath is called the Monkey Temple because hundreds of rhesus macaques live on the wooded hill, considered holy by devotees. Legend says they grew from lice in the hair of Manjushri, the bodhisattva who drained the valley. They are used to people but can grab food and bags, so keep snacks hidden and do not feed them.

faqs.q: Can elderly people visit Swayambhunath without climbing the steps?
faqs.a: Yes. Cars can drive to the western entrance, where a car park sits close to the top and a much shorter flight of steps leads to the stupa platform. It still involves some stairs, so very limited mobility is difficult. Our drivers drop guests as close as possible and the guide walks at their pace.

faqs.q: What do the eyes on Swayambhunath stupa mean?
faqs.a: The eyes painted on all four sides of the tower are the eyes of the Buddha, watching over the valley in every direction. The dot between them is the third eye of wisdom, and the curled sign below, often mistaken for a nose, is the Nepali numeral one, a symbol of unity and the single path to enlightenment.

faqs.q: Is Swayambhunath a Hindu or a Buddhist temple?
faqs.a: Swayambhunath is a Buddhist stupa, but Hindus worship here too, a mix typical of the Kathmandu Valley. The Harati temple beside the stupa honours a goddess revered by both faiths, and Hindu shrines stand on the platform. Indian Hindu families visit freely, and no part of the main platform is closed to people of other religions.

faqs.q: How far is Swayambhunath from Thamel?
faqs.a: Swayambhunath is about 3 km west of Thamel, around 15 minutes by car or taxi for NPR 300 to 400, or a 40 to 50 minute walk across the Bishnumati River. From Kathmandu Durbar Square it is about 2.5 km. Ask your driver for the east gate to climb the stairway or the western entrance to skip it.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Swayambhunath?
faqs.a: Early morning from 6 to 8 am is quiet, cool and full of local worshippers, while late afternoon gives the best light over the valley and sunset. October to February brings the clearest views, sometimes with the Himalaya to the north. Buddha Jayanti in April or May and the Newar month of Gunla in July and August are especially busy.

faqs.q: How long does a Swayambhunath visit take?
faqs.a: Allow 1.5 to 2 hours for the climb, the stupa, the shrines and the view, or 3 hours if you add Amideva Buddha Park and the hill circuit. Many travellers combine it with Kathmandu Durbar Square on the same half day, as the two are only 2.5 km apart.

faqs.q: Was Swayambhunath damaged in the 2015 earthquake?
faqs.a: Yes. The 25 April 2015 earthquake damaged several structures on the hill, including parts of the shrines around the main platform, though the stupa itself survived. Much has since been repaired and rebuilt, and the site is fully open to visitors. Occasional restoration work may close small areas, so check current status before you travel.
